title: Objection: Revelation's 'Forever and Ever' and the Undying Worm
hook: Doesn't 'the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever' settle the matter?
tldr: Revelation's 'forever and ever' smoke and Jesus' undying worm borrow from Isaiah. Isaiah used them for Edom's permanent ruin and for corpses that worms consume. Edom's 'forever' smoke stopped long ago, and Isaiah's worms eat dead bodies. So the images teach a judgment that is final and irreversible. They need not mean living people suffering without end.
big_idea: Revelation's smoke and worms are Isaiah's pictures of final ruin.

points.title: Edom's smoke 'forever' stopped
points.text: Isaiah said Edom's fire would never be quenched and its smoke would rise forever. Yet owls and ravens were to nest there. Edom is long desolate, not still burning. Revelation 14:11 borrows this exact picture.

points.title: The worm eats corpses
points.text: Isaiah 66:24 describes dead bodies. The worm and fire keep working until nothing is left. Jesus quotes this verse in Mark 9:48 to describe Gehenna.

points.title: 'Unquenchable' means unstoppable
points.text: God threatened an unquenchable fire in Jerusalem's gates. It burned the city in 586 BC and then went out. 'Not quenched' means no one can put it out until it has done its work.

points.title: Revelation 20:10 names three
points.text: Only the devil, the beast and the false prophet are said to be tormented forever. Many scholars, such as Beale, read the beast and false prophet as symbols of empires and false religion. For humans, the lake is 'the second death'.

points.title: Gates never shut
points.text: After the lake of fire, the city's gates stay open, kings once at war with God bring their glory in, and the leaves heal the nations. Universalists such as Jersak see hope here. Conditionalists disagree.

points.title: Torment before the Lamb
points.text: Revelation 14:10 places the torment 'in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb'. Basanos first meant a touchstone for testing gold, which some read as a judgment-scene trial.

sections.summary: Defenders of eternal conscious torment call Revelation 14:11 and 20:10 their clearest texts. The smoke of torment rises 'forever and ever', and there is 'no rest day or night'. D. A. Carson asks why John would mention no rest if destruction was already complete. Crossway argues that annihilation contradicts both verse 10's torment and verse 11's continuing unrest.

John draws on Isaiah 34:9-10. Edom's streams become pitch, the fire is 'not quenched night or day', and its smoke rises forever. In the same breath, Isaiah says the land will lie desolate for generations, with owls and ravens nesting in it. Commentators call this hyperbole for complete, lasting destruction. Barnes noted that John copied this image to describe the future woes of the wicked.

In Revelation 19:3 heaven shouts that Babylon's smoke 'goes up forever and ever'. Yet the previous chapter says Babylon is thrown down 'never to be found again' (Revelation 18:21). The ESV Global Study Bible reads the smoke as a symbol of permanent judgment. The rising smoke is evidence that the destruction has happened and will never be reversed.

sections.h: The lake of fire and the second death
sections.summary: Revelation 20:10 says the devil, beast and false prophet 'will be tormented day and night forever and ever'. Then Death and Hades are thrown in, which can only mean their abolition. Anyone not in the book of life follows. John defines the lake: 'This is the second death.' Some conditionalists hold that the devil may suffer while human beings die. Others read every figure as symbolic.

In Mark 9:48 Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24, where people look on 'the dead bodies' of rebels. The worm will not die and the fire will not be quenched. The Hebrew and Greek say 'not', not 'never'. Fudge reads the picture as total consumption: maggots feed while anything remains. GotQuestions and Monergism read it as an image of unending agony.

Basanizo, 'torment', comes from basanos, a dark touchstone used to test gold. It came to mean judicial examination, then torture. Revelation 14:10 sets the scene before the holy angels and the Lamb, a courtroom picture. Universalist writers read this as a refining trial. Traditional commentators read it as punishment. The word alone does not decide the question of duration.

After the lake of fire, the new Jerusalem's gates are never shut (Revelation 21:25). The 'kings of the earth', earlier God's enemies, bring their glory in. The tree's leaves heal the nations, and the invitation still says 'Come'. Bradley Jersak and Al Kimel see a hopeful possibility here, not a guarantee. Others stress that the unclean stay outside (21:27; 22:15).

mythfact.myth: 'Its smoke rises forever' must mean a fire that burns forever.
mythfact.fact: Isaiah used those words for Edom, which would lie desolate with owls nesting in it. The phrase described a ruin that was permanent, not a fire still burning.

mythfact.myth: The undying worm feeds on living souls.
mythfact.fact: Isaiah 66:24, which Jesus quotes, describes 'dead bodies'. Worms and fire keep consuming them until nothing remains.

mythfact.myth: Revelation 20:10 says every lost human is tormented forever.
mythfact.fact: The verse names the devil, the beast and the false prophet. For humans, John calls the lake 'the second death' (20:14-15; 21:8).

terms.meaning: Greek 'to the ages of the ages'. Apocalyptic language for permanence. Isaiah 34:10 uses similar wording for Edom's ruin.
A touchstone for testing gold. It came to mean judicial examination and then torment.
John's own name for the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14; 21:8).
Fire no one can put out until it finishes its work, like the fire that burned Jerusalem (Jeremiah 17:27).

quotes.text: And the smoke of their torment will rise for ever and ever. There will be no rest day or night for those who worship the beast and its image.
It will not be quenched night or day; its smoke will rise forever. From generation to generation it will lie desolate.
On no day will its gates ever be shut, for there will be no night there.

verses.role: Smoke of torment forever, no rest day or night. The objection's main text, echoing Isaiah 34.
Edom's unquenched fire and smoke 'forever'. The land then lies desolate and is inhabited by wild birds.
Babylon's smoke rises forever, though Babylon is never to be found again.
The devil, beast and false prophet are tormented forever and ever.
Death and Hades are thrown in. The lake is 'the second death'.
Worm and fire consume 'dead bodies'. Jesus' source for Mark 9:48.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's undying worm and unquenched fire for Gehenna.
An 'unquenchable' fire that burned Jerusalem and then went out.
The city's gates are never shut, even after the lake of fire.
The leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.

quiz.q: Which Old Testament passage did John borrow for 'smoke rising forever'?
quiz.why: Isaiah 34:10 says Edom's smoke rises forever, yet the land lies desolate with wild birds nesting there.

quiz.q: In Isaiah 66:24, what does the worm feed on?
quiz.why: Isaiah describes the 'dead bodies' of rebels. Jesus quotes this verse in Mark 9:48.

quiz.q: What does John call the lake of fire?
quiz.why: Revelation 20:14 and 21:8 say plainly: 'This is the second death.'

reflect: If Isaiah's 'forever' smoke described a finished ruin, what do you think John wanted persecuted readers to feel?

objections.claim: Revelation 14:11 says the smoke of their torment rises forever and they have no rest day or night. That is endless conscious suffering.
objections.strongest: Carson: why mention 'no rest day or night' if the destruction is already finished? The verse pairs torment (v.10) with ongoing unrest (v.11). Crossway argues annihilation contradicts both lines. Plain reading favors endless conscious torment.
objections.response: John is quoting Isaiah 34:10, where Edom's fire is 'not quenched night or day' and 'its smoke will rise forever'. In the same breath Isaiah says the land lies desolate and wild birds nest in it, so the fire was not literally burning. The image says the judgment is complete and irreversible. Conditionalists such as Justin Gravatt read 'no rest' as unrelenting suffering that ends in destruction, like Sodom's smoke rising after its people were dead (Genesis 19:28). The verse also speaks of beast-worshippers in an apocalyptic scene, not a timeless account of every lost soul.

objections.claim: Revelation 20:10 explicitly says 'they will be tormented day and night forever and ever'. No clearer statement exists.
objections.strongest: The text assumes the continued presence of the beast and false prophet, who were thrown in a thousand years earlier (19:20). Calling the torment 'symbolic annihilation' is imported into the text, not drawn from it. Matthew 25:41 says humans share the devil's fire.
objections.response: The verse names three figures: the devil, the beast and the false prophet. Many commentators, including Beale, read the beast and false prophet as oppressive empire and false religion. Institutions cannot feel pain. Then Death and Hades, also abstractions, are thrown in, which must mean their end. For humans John uses a different phrase: the lake is 'the second death'. Some conditionalists accept endless torment for the devil but not for humans. Universalists add that Revelation still shows the gates open afterwards. Either way, 20:10 does not state human torment.

objections.claim: Jesus said 'their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched'. Undying worms mean an undying victim.
objections.strongest: Jesus repeats the line as a refrain in Mark 9, warning his followers. GotQuestions and many preachers read the worm as inner torment or conscience that never ceases. An undying worm needs something undying to feed on.
objections.response: Jesus is quoting Isaiah 66:24, which describes 'dead bodies' of rebels looked on by the living. Worms there consume corpses, and the fire burns them. 'Not quenched' means unstoppable, not eternal. Jeremiah 17:27 threatened an unquenchable fire in Jerusalem's gates, and it went out once the city was burned. The Hebrew and Greek say the worm does 'not' die, not that it 'never' dies. The picture is total, shameful destruction no one can stop. It does not describe a living person suffering forever.

objections.claim: 'Forever and ever' (to the ages of the ages) is the Bible's strongest phrase for endlessness. Revelation uses it for God himself.
objections.strongest: Revelation 4:9-10 and 15:7 use the same phrase for God who lives forever and ever. If it is weakened for the wicked, it is weakened for God. John chose the strongest possible wording on purpose.
objections.response: The phrase takes its force from its subject. God lives forever and ever because God is immortal. Babylon's smoke also goes up 'forever and ever' (19:3), yet Babylon is thrown down 'never to be found again' (18:21). Isaiah 34:10 uses matching language for Edom, a land that 'none will pass through forever and ever' while wild animals live there. In apocalyptic writing, smoke that rises forever is a memorial to a finished judgment. Its meaning comes from Isaiah, not from a word count.

objections.claim: Isaiah 34 was a historical judgment, but Revelation describes the final one. You cannot shrink final judgment to Edom's level.
objections.strongest: Edom was literal hyperbole for a nation. Revelation 14 concerns persons who are 'tormented with fire and sulfur', and torment requires conscious subjects. Even if the smoke echoes Isaiah, the torment word adds suffering that Isaiah lacks.
objections.response: Conditionalists do not deny the torment. Revelation 14:10 describes real, conscious suffering in the presence of the Lamb at judgment. What the passage adds to Isaiah is the experience of judgment. It does not add endless duration, which still comes only from the borrowed smoke image. The scene is also set before the Lamb and holy angels, a courtroom, not a description of where the lost remain forever. Basanos first meant testing on a touchstone. Some universalists read it as refining, though that reading is debated.

objections.claim: The 'open gates' argument is wishful. Revelation 21:27 and 22:15 say the impure stay outside the city.
objections.strongest: John says nothing unclean will ever enter the city and that dogs, sorcerers and liars are outside. Healing of the nations refers to the redeemed peoples' flourishing, not to rescue from the lake of fire. Universalism reads hope into silence.
objections.response: This is a fair point, and readers who reject eternal torment disagree among themselves here. Conditionalists agree that those outside are excluded and then perish. Universalists such as Jersak and Kimel point to tensions John leaves in the text. The 'kings of the earth' who fought the Lamb (19:19) bring their glory into the city (21:24). The gates are never shut. The leaves heal the nations. 'Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may enter' (22:14), and the invitation 'Come' still sounds (22:17). Kimel calls this a hope, not a guarantee.

objections.claim: Heaven shouts 'Hallelujah' over the rising smoke. The saints will forever celebrate the endless punishment of the wicked.
objections.strongest: Revelation 19:1-3 shows God's people praising him because her smoke goes up forever. Endless justice displayed before the redeemed seems to be part of the book's vision of glory.
objections.response: The celebration in Revelation 19 is over Babylon, a system that killed the saints (19:2). Heaven rejoices that oppression is ended for good. In John's day, Revelation's warnings were addressed to Christians tempted to worship the beast to survive (14:9-12). The vivid images warned them against compromise and assured them of vindication. The smoke shows that Babylon will never rise again. It does not ask believers to enjoy watching people suffer forever.
